children: By Bertrand Benoit

BERLIN-German Chancellor Friedrich Merz pledged to forge ahead with an unpopular economic overhaul despite his collapsing popularity, misgivings among his coalition partners, and a string of electoral routs that have raised doubts about his political future.

Monday's comments sought to bring an end to weeks of debate about how long Merz can keep together his coalition, in office for just a year-and-a-half. The chancellor's electoral setbacks culminated on Sunday in the worst-ever result for his Christian Democratic Union and the latest wins for parties on the far left and far right.

"We want to move forward with the reform process, but we know people are concerned and afraid and we must give them answers," Merz said. "The extremists suggest that there are simple solutions, but anyone who has been in government knows these don't exist."

Merz's CDU won't be represented in the parliament of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, a small Eastern state, after failing to clear a 5% vote threshold on Sunday-a result Merz described as "a disaster." This was the first time the CDU had fallen under the 5% mark.

The election's winner was the far-right Alternative for Germany, or AfD, with 38.7% of the vote. Unlike in Saxony-Anhalt, another Eastern state, where the AfD got close to an absolute majority of votes two weeks ago, it is unlikely to govern in the state because left-leaning parties have more seats.

Meanwhile, in the city-state of Berlin, the Left Party, successor to the former East-German ruling party, emerged victorious with more than a quarter of the votes, putting it in pole position to head the German capital's next government.

The Left has pledged to expropriate residential properties from large commercial landlords in a bid to keep rents low. The party has received support from groups that have been accused of promoting terror and antisemitism.

"I stand for the protection of Jewish life," Elif Eralp, the party's lead candidate, said on Monday after photos emerged overnight showing a representative of a U.S.-sanctioned Palestinian organization and the Lebanese-born head of one of Berlin's oldest organized-crime gangs attending a Left Party postelection party in Berlin.

Merz described the three elections of the past two weeks as a turning point, saying "we are witnessing a fundamental transformation of the party system, in Germany and in many other countries around the world." Some 40% of voters in Berlin had picked parties that aimed to topple established institutions, he added.

Merz has stressed the need for stable leadership in Europe's largest economy amid persistent economic headwinds for Europe, including rising oil prices and financing costs, and mounting threats from Russia. After launching investment programs to rearm the country and fix its crumbling infrastructure, his government has begun work on overhauling its generous but underfunded welfare system.

It wants to pass a package of bills by the end of the year, including modest tax cuts, an overhaul of the country's state health-insurance system, and changes to its pension system that economists have said are needed to keep the system funded in the medium term amid stagnant growth and a rapid rise in the number of retirees.

On the upside for Merz, there are no significant state elections until late June, when North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany's most populous state, is widely expected to re-elect its CDU governor. This gives the chancellor a few months of respite on the electoral front. Already the most unpopular leader in German postwar history, he doesn't have much further to fall in polls.

Merz is also benefiting from a standoff between left-leaning and right-leaning CDU leaders, who have been unable to agree on a possible successor as chancellor and CDU chairman. The party is split between the original supporters of Merz's tough reformist agendas, who have lost faith in his ability to implement it, and former centrist backers of ex-Chancellor Angela Merkel, who always mistrusted Merz's more right-wing positions.

Both camps last week agreed to bury the hatchet-for now-as all of the party's eight state governors agreed to write a joint letter that didn't mention Merz by name but expressed support for the chancellor.

Quashing mounting unrest in the party's grassroots could prove harder, especially in the small Eastern states and large urban centers where the CDU is fast becoming marginalized, as younger voters turn to the far right and the far left.

Merz could also struggle to keep his junior partner, the center-left Social Democratic Party, on board with his planned economic changes, especially a proposal to end a highly popular scheme that has allowed many to retire four years before reaching the statutory retirement age of 67.

Many SPD functionaries think the party's coalition with the conservatives has cost it support and see its future is in a more robustly left-wing course. Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil, who is fending off his own challengers for the party chair, said on Monday he remained committed to the coalition but would need changes to Merz's economic plans. The SPD, he said, would hold a convention in December to discuss adjustments to its policies in light of the recent elections.
Should the SPD refuse to back his economic package, Merz should call a vote of confidence in parliament, Dennis Thering, the head of the CDU in Hamburg, told a German broadcaster.
